comments.body:
Thanks for the report!

First note that JAX makes no promises about respecting the `__array__` attribute of objects passed to it: this is accessed by NumPy, which JAX falls back to here: https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/c3b20ca7eaf18550062b1fd0b05ade3664333ab6/jax/_src/numpy/array_constructors.py#L255-L260

I think the issue here is that `jnp.array` does not expect user-defined pytrees as arguments, and so the behavior in this case is not well defined.

I think the best solution would probably be to detect these unexpected arguments to `jax.array`, and raise an explicit error. Then all three of your cases would return consistent results (i.e. an error).

What do you think?

If it were up to me, if  `jax.numpy.array` is going to fallback to `numpy.array` then I would assume it to be equivalent. I'm not actually sure flattening should be involved here at all, since flattening *is* for pytrees. The closest thing numpy does is for iterables or nested iterables beings stacked into nd-arrays. I might expect  `jax.numpy.array` to do something like the following:

* if has `__jax_array__`, call directly and then cast to desired dtype (if not None)
* elif has `__array__`, fallback to numpy, convert to jax.Array with desired dtype (if not None)
* ... other array interfaces?
* elif has `__iter__`, follow similar conventions as numpy, but supporting jax arrays, tracers, etc.

> If it were up to me, if `jax.numpy.array` is going to fallback to `numpy.array` then I would assume it to be equivalent.

The only reason we fall back to `numpy` at all is for performance reasons: if you have a large nested iterable of Python scalars, dispatching to `lax.concatenate` ends up being very slow, so we detect this case and call `np.asarray` to avoid that. And we know it's not equivalent (look at my 4-year-old TODO in the code linked above) but our hands are tied by peformance issues.

Likewise, the problem with strictly following the logic that you propose is also performance-related. We could check for `__jax_array__`, `__array__`, `__iter__`, etc. for every entry in a nested list of containers passed to `jnp.array`, but that adds a *lot* of unnecessary overhead in common cases, just to handle very rare corner cases.

`jnp.array` is one of the most frequently used APIs in JAX, so adding that amount of additional logic is difficult to do, and there are already tradeoffs between performance and semantics.

> __jax_array__, __array__, __iter__, etc. for every entry in a nested list of containers passed to jnp.array

I could be mistaken, but from the current code I think it basically already does this. If the object is a list/tuple it calls `jax.numpy.array` recursively, which repeat checks `__jax_array__`, `__cuda_array_interface__`, etc, and flattens and does instance check on every leaf. If it is pure python scalars this should only flatten once, but if there is mixed jax arrays in there then the number of flattenings could scale exponentially with the depth of the nesting, since it repeats it for every recursion.

The only change I would really be asking is that it not impose a default dtype if it is going to fallback to numpy, unless one was given by the user.

> The only change I would really be asking is that it not impose a default dtype if it is going to fallback to numpy, unless one was given by the user.

The reason we pass the dtype here is for JIT invariance. NumPy's dtype promotion semantics differ from JAX's dtype promotion semantics: this means that if we allow NumPy to determine the type for non-traced inputs, and use JAX to determine the type for traced inputs, we could end up with different dtypes depending on whether an operation is JIT compiled or not. That kind of breakage of jit invariance can be quite problematic, so one of the prime design goals for JAX APIs is to avoid that.

All that to say, we need to pass a dtype to `np.array` here.

Now a change we could make is to modify the `tree_flatten` call to inspect each element and determine if it is a custom pytree; then we could possibly do a better job of respecting the interplay between `__array__`, `__jax_array__`, and `tree_flatten` that you mention above.

As I mentioned, though, this would add extra overhead to *every* call to `jnp.array`, and that is an API that is very widely used. The question is whether it's worth adding extra overhead to more-or-less **every** JAX program in order to handle this rare corner case more consistently. It's not obvious to me that that would be a net win.

What do you think?

I tried something like the following change when narrowing down the cause, basically just not setting a dtype if there are no leaves.

```python
  if dtype is None:
    # Use lattice_result_type rather than result_type to avoid canonicalization.
    # Otherwise, weakly-typed inputs would have their dtypes canonicalized.
    try:
      dtype = (
          dtypes.lattice_result_type(*leaves)[0]
          if leaves
          else dtypes.default_float_dtype()
      )
  ...
```

to

```python
  if dtype is None and leaves:
    # Use lattice_result_type rather than result_type to avoid canonicalization.
    # Otherwise, weakly-typed inputs would have their dtypes canonicalized.
    try:
      dtype = dtypes.lattice_result_type(*leaves)[0]
  ...
```

In my current use cases a custom `__array__` would only come into play in two scenarios:

- An object that *is* a leaf type, and therefor is the only leaf when flattened.
- An object that is static, neither being a leaf nor having any children.

I currently cannot think of a scenario where an object would support `__array__` while also being a pytree with children. I guess my question would be what case is being handled by `default_float_dtype()` when there are no leaves.
does `jnp.array(x).dtype` and `jax.jit(jnp.array)(x).dtype` match for the cases of interest when you make these changes?

Yes, for the cases compatible with `jit` (the second case above), `__array__` returns with the same dtype either way. In the first case, the argument is not yet a jax array. I get your concern about invariance when tracing vs not, but also I think for these kind of cases `jax.jit(jnp.array)` is a bit special because we have to be able to get objects into valid jax arrays *before* calling jitted functions.

My inclination here is to not change anything. I say that for a few reasons:

1. `jnp.array` is used in many places, and past experiences show that *any* change to its logic is difficult to land, with a likelihood of rollbacks due to unanticipated effects of the change.
3. We don't have any explicitly documented support for objects that define `__array__`, and so making changes in service of a particular case of that seems likely to overlook other cases, unless we were to address it comprehensively.
4. The corner case you bring up (where tree flattening, `__jax_array__`, and `__array__` interact in ways that are not well defined according to the function's specification) does not strike me as one that is particularly common.
5. As I mentioned above, this is performance-critical code because it is used in many places inside and outside of JAX, and so the deeply-nested checks required to catch corner cases like these will be too costly. We already have a years-old TODO note related to similar inconsistencies in the exact line of code that is relevant here, and it's never risen to the level of something we've felt the need to address.

For all those reasons, I'd prefer to avoid churn with this code, and close this as working as expected (with acknowledgement that the status quo is imperfect). Any thoughts?

Well, I can sympathize maintaining these kind of high-entropy functions that try to handle a grab bag of different types of inputs, possibly with competing goals. The worst case would be if there was some ambiguity as to what even *should* happen, and even though I don't think thats the case here there does seem to be quite a bit to consider. Also there are  explicit workarounds, like manually going through numpy first. So it makes sense closing this in favor of a more comprehensive solution down the line.

But I would also say that getting data into jax arrays is prerequisite to downstream stuff, and the docstring *does* state that `__array__` is one of the supported protocols.

> and the docstring _does_ state that `__array__` is one of the supported protocols.

Thanks for pointing that out – we should probably remove that from the docstring, because it's inaccurate. For example, if you have a pytree that defines the `__array__` object and you pass it to `jnp.array` under JIT, the `__array__` protocol will be ignored.

I think there is a fix we should make here, in particular this line: https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/5466dd7b6d8b49e794a741adcbeadde6d8b6cb32/jax/_src/numpy/array_constructors.py#L229

I believe the intent here was to use `tree_flatten` to iterate through the values in nested lists and tuples, but if something registered as a pytree is passed to `jnp.array`, it will also iterate into its leaves. This is incorrect behavior I think; instead we should change it to be something like this:
```python
leaves, treedef = tree_util.tree_flatten(object, is_leaf=lambda x: not isinstance(x, (tuple, list))
```
With this change, all three of your objects would error when passed to `jnp.array`, because none of them are valid inputs to `jnp.array` – I think this would be the unambiguous correct behavior here.

Actually, with this change by itself I think all three would work with `jnp.array`, and the second two work with `jax.jit(jnp.array)`. If every non-list/tuple is considered a leaf, then they all are seen as leaves and the rest of the logic works out the same as numpy arrays. Why do you say they would result in error?

> Why do you say they would result in error?

Currently it does because the code does not dispatch to `__array__` for arbitrary objects. If your objects defined `__jax_array__`, then I believe it would work.

With [#33042](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/pull/33042), your code works as you would expect after one small change: if you define your classes like this `a = A((1,2), np.dtype('complex64'))`, i.e. using the actual dtype rather than the scalar type (as required by `np.dtype`).

With this change, running your code results in this:
```
A.__array__(None, copy=True)
B.__array__(None, copy=True)
C.__array__(None, copy=True)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A.__array__(complex64, copy=False)
C.__array__(complex64, copy=False)
B.__array__(complex64, copy=False)
```

issue.body:
### Description

This issue is to report a difference in behavior of `jax.numpy.array(a)` versus `numpy.array(a)` in determination of a dtype when using `__array__()`. Numpy calls `a.__array__(None)`, but I believe jax does something like the following:

*  `flatten(a)` -> `[x, y, z]`
* get `dtype = x.dtype` if there's at least one leaf, otherwise chooses `dtype = float32|float64`
* *then* call `a.__array__(dtype)`

```python
# test_array.py
import numpy as np
from jax import numpy as jnp
import jax

class A:
  # custom class with an __array__, by default JAX treats this class as a leaf
  def __init__(self, shape, dtype):
    self.shape = shape
    self.dtype = dtype

  def __array__(self, dtype = None, *, copy = False):
    print(f"{type(self).__name__}.__array__({dtype}, {copy=})")
    return np.zeros(self.shape, self.dtype)
```

```python
@jax.tree_util.register_static
class B(A):
  # register the class as purely static (no children/leaves)
  def __hash__(self):
    return hash((self.shape, self.dtype))

  def __eq__(self, other):
    return type(self) is type(other) and self.shape == other.shape and self.dtype == other.dtype
```

```python
@jax.tree_util.register_pytree_node_class
class C(B):
  # register the class with a dummy leaf with the correct dtype
  def tree_flatten(self):
    return [np.zeros(0, self.dtype)], self

  @classmethod
  def tree_unflatten(cls, static, dynamic):
    return static
```


```python
a = A((1,2), np.complex64)
b = B((1,2), np.complex64)
c = C((1,2), np.complex64)

for x in [a, b, c]:
  y = np.array(x)
  assert y.dtype == x.dtype

print('-'*80)

for x in [a, c, b]: # c tested before b, since b causes error
  y = jnp.array(x)
  assert y.dtype == x.dtype
```

```text
A.__array__(None, copy=True)
B.__array__(None, copy=True)
C.__array__(None, copy=True)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A.__array__(complex64, copy=False)
C.__array__(complex64, copy=False)
B.__array__(float32, copy=False)
v313/lib/python3.13/site-packages/jax/_src/numpy/array_constructors.py:248: ComplexWarning: Casting complex values to real discards the imaginary part
  out = np.asarray(object, dtype=dtype)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test_array.py", line 44, in <module>
    assert y.dtype == x.dtype
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AssertionError
```

issue.body:
Fix handling of pytrees within `jnp.array` and `jnp.asarray`.

Previously, the logic meant for probing nested lists and tuples would traverse into the leaves of custom pytrees; this was unintentional. This change should make the handling of pytrees within `jnp.array` much more predictable.

Addresses #32725
